briefing.headline: Get fluent. Or stay slow forever.
body: The terminal is a text interface to your filesystem and your processes. Everything you'll do here you could also do with Finder and Activity Monitor — slower, with worse tools, and with no way to script it. Most PMs know three commands: cd, ls, clear. That's not enough.
This is a practice module. Read the step, type the commands yourself — don't paste — and don't move on until the verify passes. Fluency comes from repetition, not from understanding.

reference.title: Navigation cheat sheet
reference.content:
pwd            Where am I?
ls             What's here?
ls -la         List with detail, including hidden files
cd <path>      Change directory
cd ~           Go home
cd ..          Go up one level
cd -           Go back to previous directory

reference.title: File operations cheat sheet
reference.content:
touch <file>           Create empty file
mkdir <dir>            Create directory
mkdir -p a/b/c         Create nested path
cp <src> <dst>         Copy file
cp -r <src> <dst>      Copy directory
mv <src> <dst>         Move or rename
rm <file>              Delete file
rm -r <dir>            Delete directory and contents

reference.title: Path shortcuts
reference.content:
~ is your home directory (/Users/<you>).
. is the current directory.
.. is the parent directory.
- (with cd) is the previous directory you were in.

reference.title: Pipes and redirects
reference.content:
cmd1 | cmd2     Send cmd1 output as input to cmd2
cmd > file      Write output to file (overwrites)
cmd >> file     Append output to file
cmd 2> file     Write errors to file

reference.title: How to get unstuck
reference.content:
Ctrl + C — cancel the current command.
Ctrl + D — exit a shell or program waiting for input.
q — quit man, less, top, and most full-screen terminal programs.
Cmd + K (iTerm2) — clear the screen.

reference.title: "No such file or directory"
reference.content: Either the path is wrong or you're not where you think you are. Run pwd to check, then ls to see what's actually there. Tab-completion is your friend — start typing a name and press Tab.

reference.title: "Permission denied"
reference.content: You don't have rights to that file or directory. Don't sudo your way past it — that's how people break their systems. Stop and check: are you in the right place? Is this a system file you shouldn't be touching?

completion.headline: M1 complete.
completion.body: You can navigate, create, read, move, and delete from the command line. Next up: M2 — VS Code.

steps.title: Where you are, what's here
steps.body: Two questions every terminal session starts with: where am I, and what's in this directory? Two commands answer both. ls -la adds detail — file sizes, dates, and entries that begin with a dot (hidden files).
steps.verify: pwd prints a path. ls prints a list. ls -la prints a longer list including . and ...

steps.title: Move around
steps.body: cd changes directory. ~ is home. .. is one level up. - is wherever you were last. You go nowhere without these four.
steps.code:
cd ~
pwd
cd Desktop
pwd
cd ..
pwd
cd -
pwd
steps.verify: Each pwd prints a different path that matches what you'd expect from the cd before it.

steps.title: Make a workspace
steps.body: Create a folder in your home directory to play in for the rest of this module. mkdir makes directories.
steps.code:
cd ~
mkdir mve-practice
cd mve-practice
pwd

steps.title: Create files
steps.body: touch creates an empty file. Multiple files in one command — separate with spaces.
steps.code:
touch hello.txt
touch a.txt b.txt c.txt
ls

steps.title: Put content in, read it back
steps.body: echo prints a string. > redirects that output into a file instead of the screen. >> appends. cat dumps the whole file. head and tail show just the top or bottom.
steps.code:
echo "line one" > poem.txt
echo "line two" >> poem.txt
echo "line three" >> poem.txt
cat poem.txt
head -1 poem.txt
tail -1 poem.txt
steps.verify: cat prints all three lines. head -1 prints only line one. tail -1 prints only line three.
steps.trouble: If cat shows only line three: you used > instead of >> on the second and third lines and overwrote the file each time.

steps.title: Copy and rename
steps.body: cp copies. mv moves — and a move within the same directory is a rename.
steps.code:
cp poem.txt poem-backup.txt
mv poem-backup.txt poem-v2.txt
ls

steps.title: Delete
steps.body: rm deletes a file. rm -r deletes a directory and everything in it. There is no Trash. There is no undo. Read the command before pressing Enter.
steps.trouble: If you ever type something like rm -rf / or rm -rf ~ — stop. Don't press Enter. Backspace it out. These commands wipe your computer.

steps.title: Wildcards
steps.body: * matches any sequence of characters. ? matches one character. Lets you operate on groups of files at once.
steps.code:
touch one.txt two.txt three.md four.md
ls *.txt
ls *.md
ls ?ne.txt
steps.verify: First ls shows only .txt files, second shows only .md files, third shows only one.txt.

steps.title: Pipes
steps.body: | takes the output of the command on its left and feeds it as input to the command on its right. This is how you chain commands. Most real terminal use is small commands piped together.
steps.verify: First command prints the first 5 lines of ls -la. Second command prints a single number — the count of files in this directory.

steps.title: Processes and stopping things
steps.body: A process is a running program. top shows them live, sorted by CPU. The skill you actually need: stopping a command that's stuck or running too long. Ctrl + C cancels. Use it constantly.
notes: Watch the list update for a few seconds.
Run ping google.com — it'll keep pinging forever.
steps.verify: You exited top with q and stopped ping with Ctrl + C.

steps.title: Environment variables
steps.body: Variables your shell knows about. $PATH is the most important — it's the list of directories where your shell looks for commands. When something says "command not found", that means: "I looked everywhere on PATH and didn't find it."
steps.verify: Each prints a value. $HOME matches your home directory. $SHELL is /bin/zsh.

steps.title: Get help
steps.body: man <command> opens the manual page (press q to quit). <command> --help prints a quick summary. When you forget what a flag does, this is the answer — not Google.
notes: Scroll with arrow keys or space bar.
Search inside the page with / followed by your search term, then Enter.
steps.verify: You opened the man page for ls and quit it with q.

steps.title: Clean up
steps.body: Delete the practice directory. You're back to a clean home directory.
steps.verify: Final ls errors with No such file or directory — because the directory is gone. That's the success state.
